# Migration: v2.8 → v2.9

## Summary

v2.9 changes who owns your templates. Until now every migration copied the
scaffold's templates over yours, so tailoring one meant losing the edit at the
next upgrade. From v2.9 the templates are **seeded**: the scaffold installs a
working default, `docs/.pdocs-seed.json` records what it installed, and a later
migration updates a template only while you have not touched it — reporting it,
rather than overwriting it, once you have.

It also opens the document-type vocabulary. A project can declare its own folder
(`docs/runbooks/` carrying `type: runbook`) in `.project-docs.json` and the lint
accepts it.

**What changes in your tree:** `scripts/pdocs/` and `docs/SCHEMA.md` are
replaced, `docs/.pdocs-seed.json` is added, both version markers are set, and
Prettier is run over your templates (skippable). No document you wrote is
touched.

## This migration is a script

One command does the whole migration. Every phase verifies itself, and any
failure stops the run with a non-zero exit and a named reason — including
failures the script did not anticipate.

**Why, in two sentences you can check yourself.** A guard computed in one shell
block and consumed in the next runs in a **different process**, so it protects
nothing. A check whose only output is an echoed string cannot fail a run. One
process and real exit codes make both impossible rather than discouraged.

## What's New

- **`docs/.pdocs-seed.json`** — the seed manifest, shaped
  `{ "version": "<the release you migrated to>", "files": { "<path>": "<sha256>" } }`.
  The hashes are of the bytes **in your project**, not the scaffold's — see
  [What adoption does not do](#what-adoption-does-not-do).
- **`scripts/pdocs/seed.ts`** — reads it back and decides, per file: `update`,
  `install`, `keep-modified`, `keep-unknown`, `keep-deleted`. **Nothing calls it
  yet**; it is the API the next migration uses. The record has to exist before
  there is anything to reconcile against.
- **`lint.types` in `.project-docs.json`** — declare your own folders and the
  `type` their pages carry.
- **`pdocs find --type` now refuses an unknown type**, naming the set it knows.
  It previously returned `count: 0` at exit 0, which reads as "nothing matches".
  **This is a breaking change** for anything branching on that exit code.
- **A "Who owns which file" section in `docs/SCHEMA.md`** — **owned** (a
  migration replaces it, because code reads it), **seeded** (installed once,
  then negotiated by hash — the templates), **theirs** (never touched:
  `.project-docs.json`, `docs/index.md`, everything you write), plus
  **structural** for files carrying no content.

## What Moved / What's Removed

Nothing, in either case.

## Run it

```bash
cd <your project root>              # the directory holding .project-docs.json
SKILL_DIR=<the update-project-docs skill directory>
bun "$SKILL_DIR/migrations/scripts/migrate-v2.8-to-v2.9.ts" --dry-run
```

Set `SKILL_DIR` in the **same** block you use it in, or paste the literal path —
a shell variable does not survive into a separate command. An agent that loaded
`update-project-docs` has the directory as its "Base directory for this skill";
otherwise it is two levels above this file.

The dry run changes nothing in your project and prints what each phase would do,
including every template it would record. **Read that list.** It should name the
templates you recognise — one per category folder, plus those under
`docs/projects/TEMPLATES/`. A count of 0 stops the run by itself; a list naming
files you do not recognise means `--root` or `docsRoot` is not what you think.

Then:

```bash
bun "$SKILL_DIR/migrations/scripts/migrate-v2.8-to-v2.9.ts"
```

Commit the result, `docs/.pdocs-seed.json` included.

### Options

| Flag                 | When you need it                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--root <path>`      | The project to migrate. Defaults to the current directory.                                                                                                          |
| `--dry-run`          | Report every phase's plan; change nothing in the project.                                                                                                           |
| `--scaffold-dir <p>` | Use a scaffold you already generated instead of fetching one. Skips the network. `--scaffold` is accepted as an alias.                                              |
| `--skip-format`      | Do not run Prettier. **Required** if your project has no `npx` or does not use Prettier — otherwise the run stops rather than recording hashes it would invalidate. |
| `--re-adopt`         | Rebuild an existing manifest from the bytes on disk now. Read [If you run it twice](#if-you-run-it-twice) first — it is not always the right answer.                |

Exit codes: `0` success · `1` the migration could not complete · `2` bad
invocation.

## What it does, phase by phase

1. **Preflight** — confirms this is a project-docs tree, resolves `docsRoot`,
   requires `cookiecutter` (and `npx` unless `--skip-format`), and reports a
   dirty git tree. The dirty tree is reported, not enforced — it is your
   repository, and the report is so you can keep this migration's changes
   separable from your own.
2. **Scaffold** — generates the current template into a private temp directory,
   never into your project. A dry run generates it too: without one, the version
   phase has nothing to read and would report a number taken from your own tree.
3. **Refresh the owned files** — copies the scaffold's `scripts/pdocs/` over
   yours and replaces `docs/SCHEMA.md`, then verifies `seed.ts` and both new
   `SCHEMA.md` sections arrived. The copy **merges**: a file a later version
   removes would survive, and would need deleting explicitly. A scaffold older
   than v2.9 stops the run here.
4. **Format the templates** — Prettier, over the templates only, and **before**
   phase 5.
5. **Adopt** — records each template's sha256, counted from the parsed object. A
   count of zero stops the run.
6. **Verify** — `pdocs check` must exit 0, and `find --type nosuchtype` must
   exit 2.
7. **Version markers** — sets `docs_version` and `.project-docs.json`'s
   `version` to the release you migrated to, reporting each separately.
   `.project-docs.json` is **theirs**, so only that one value is written: the
   top-level `"version"` is patched in the file's own text — indent, array style
   and every other byte kept — and the result is parsed and checked against the
   intended object before it is written. A line-based expression once rewrote
   every nested `"version"` in it, and a re-serialisation once rewrote its
   formatting. Only when there is no top-level `"version"` to patch does the
   phase re-serialise the file, in its own indent, and the phase line says so. A
   file already at the release is not written.
8. **Cleanup** — removes the generated scaffold.

**Phase 4 before phase 5 is load-bearing.** Phase 5 records the bytes of each
template. Formatting one afterwards leaves it not matching its own recorded
hash, so the next migration reads it as edited by you and never updates it again
— the whole mechanism opted out of, for files nobody touched. The script
re-checks this at the end of every run and fails if it does not hold, so the
ordering is enforced rather than merely intended.

## What adoption does not do

It compares nothing and replaces nothing. On this run nothing is known — your
project has no record of what the scaffold once installed — so every template is
adopted as it stands. A template you edited three versions ago is recorded as
though it had shipped that way. That is the honest answer, and it is why this is
a one-time adoption rather than a reconciliation. From the next migration on,
the comparison runs.

## If you run it twice

Re-running is safe. With a manifest already present the script verifies it
instead of rewriting:

- **every hash matches and nothing is unrecorded** — nothing to adopt; the rest
  of the migration still runs.
- **a hash does not match** — the run **stops** and names the file. Two
  readings, and the script cannot tell them apart:
  - **you edited that template since adopting.** This is the mechanism working.
    **Do not `--re-adopt`.** Re-adopting records your edited bytes as the
    scaffold's baseline, so the next migration reads them as untouched and
    overwrites them — destroying the edit this feature exists to protect.
  - **adoption ran before formatting**, so the record was wrong from the start.
    Here `--re-adopt` is correct: the file is not something you changed.

  If you cannot tell which, leave it. A stale entry costs you one template that
  stops being updated; a wrong `--re-adopt` costs you the edit.

- **a template is on disk but in no manifest** — the run stops and names it.
  `--re-adopt` is always right here: there is no record to lose, and without it
  that template would never be updated by any later migration.

## Optional: declare your own document type

Not part of the migration. To add `docs/runbooks/` carrying `type: runbook`, add
the folder to a tier array and name its type:

```jsonc
// .project-docs.json — the "lint" block. ADD to the existing arrays.
"workbench": ["backlog", "briefs", "...", "runbooks"],
"types": { "runbooks": "runbook" }
```

`.project-docs.json` is plain JSON — the `//` above is annotation for this page,
not something to paste, and the existing entries in `workbench` must stay.

The tier follows from the array the folder is listed in: `workbench` for the
thin checks, `durable` for the full graph tier including catalog reachability. A
declared type is lintable but not creatable — `pdocs new` ships no template for
it and says so. `docs/SCHEMA.md` has the detail.

## Cross-Reference Updates

None. No path changed and no document type was added or removed.

## Verification

The script checks all of this itself and stops on any failure, so this is what
to look for in its output rather than commands to run.

- [ ] `✓ formatted N template(s)` appears **before** `✓ recorded N template(s)`
      — unless you passed `--skip-format`, where `· skipped` and no `formatted`
      line is correct
- [ ] `✓ recorded N template(s)` — on a **re-run** this is instead
      `✓ every recorded hash still matches, and nothing is unrecorded`
- [ ] `✓ pdocs check: clean`
- [ ] `✓ unknown --type refused with exit 2`
- [ ] one line per version marker, each naming what happened to it
- [ ] `Migration complete.` and **exit 0.** The exit code is the check; the
      lines above tell you which phase produced it
- [ ] `git check-ignore -v docs/.pdocs-seed.json` prints nothing, and the file
      is committed. **The script cannot check this**, and a manifest that never
      reaches the repository cannot be read next time.
